                                   PUC PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                   §
                                                                        OF TEXAS
                                                  §
                                                  §

                       CHOLLA, INC’S SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS

                             I.      STATEMENT OF INTEREST

       Cholla, Inc. (“Cholla”) is a Texas-based developer of large-scale load infrastructure
operating in the ERCOT power region. Cholla develops sites for data centers, industrial facilities,
and other high-demand energy users, and has direct experience navigating the ERCOT large load
interconnection process on behalf of end-use customers and project sponsors.

       Through its direct participation in multiple interconnection requests, Cholla has developed
operational expertise regarding the various iterations of ERCOT’s large load interconnection study
processes, and the financial, contractual, and timing constraints that govern large load project
development, including capital deployment decisions that are made prior to and following
interconnection study results.

       Cholla has a direct and substantial interest in this rulemaking because the proposed
financial security framework materially affects its ability to pursue, structure, and finance large
load development projects in Texas. The proposed requirement to post exceptionally large, non-
refundable financial security at an early-to-mid stage of development—before interconnection
study results are available to developers, investors, or even the relevant electric utilities—imposes
disproportionate and fundamentally unquantifiable project-level risk untethered from developer
conduct or actual cost incurrence and, as a result, materially distorts investment decision-making.

       These impacts implicate the Commission’s statutory obligation under PURA § 37.0561 to
establish interconnection standards in a manner that supports business development while
maintaining reliability and minimizing stranded infrastructure costs.

                 II.     INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF POSITION

       These supplemental comments expand upon and further develop the legal and structural

                                                 1
 concerns identified in Cholla’s initial comments on Commission Staff’s Proposal for Publication
(“PFP”). 1 The focus of these comments is narrow but fundamental: whether the proposed financial
security framework operates within the Commission’s statutory authority when evaluated under
PURA Chapters 36 and 37, and more specifically § 37.0561.

         Cholla supports the Commission’s objectives in this rulemaking. The need for meaningful
financial commitment requirements, improved queue discipline, and coordinated study processes
is well established. The transition to a more structured and disciplined interconnection framework
is necessary to address the scale of large load development currently present in ERCOT. However,
as proposed, 16 Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”) § 25.194 introduces a mechanism that extends beyond
interconnection standards and into transmission cost allocation. Specifically, the proposed rule
combines (i) the requirement to post substantial, non-refundable financial security prior to
completion of interconnection studies, with (ii) the mandatory retention and application of those
funds to reduce transmission cost recovery. Evaluated in combination, these features result in the
collection and redistribution of funds that are not necessarily tied to costs of a specific
interconnection request.

         This issue is further compounded by the absence of an explicit limitation consistent with
PURA § 35.004(c-1), which—under Senate Bill 6—applies only to interconnection agreements
executed on or after June 20, 2025. The proposed rule does not incorporate this statutory boundary.
Absent clarification, this creates a material risk that financial obligations—including financial
security, CIAC, and related interconnection costs—will be applied to projects that executed
interconnection agreements or satisfied interconnection requirements prior to that date, effectively
resulting in retroactive re-underwriting under a framework that did not exist at the time those
investments were made. Texas law disfavors such retroactive application absent clear legislative
authorization, particularly where it would impair reasonable reliance on prior regulatory
frameworks.

         This characterization cannot be resolved by labeling the financial requirement as an
“interconnection condition.” Under well-established administrative law principles, an agency’s
authority is determined by the substance and effect of the requirement, not its label. 2

1
 PUC Proj. No. 58481, Cholla Comments on Proposal for Publication (Apr. 7, 2026).
2
 See e.g., U.S. Dept. of Labor v. Kast Metals Corp., 744 F.2d 1145, 1149 (5th Cir. 1984) (noting that courts are not
bound by an administrative agency’s classification of its own action and that the substance, not the label, of the agency

                                                           2
 Interconnection conditions must be grounded in the operational, technical, or cost impacts of the
specific connection and must fall within the scope of applicable statutory authority, including
PURA § 35.004(c-1), which governs the recovery of interconnection-related costs from large load
customers subject to PURA § 37.0561 and, as limited by SB 6, applies prospectively to
interconnection agreements executed on or after June 20, 2025. To the extent that such
requirements result in charges to a customer, those charges must also be consistent with PURA §§
36.003 and 36.004, including the requirement that rates be just, reasonable, and not unduly
discriminatory.

        Here, the proposed structure departs from those principles. The proposed rule would
require financial security to be posted before study completion, allow retention of funds
irrespective of whether corresponding costs are incurred, and direct retained amounts to reduce
system-wide transmission cost recovery. In doing so, it operates not as a project-specific
interconnection safeguard, but as a mechanism for allocating costs across the broader body of
ratepayers in a manner that is not tied to identified system impacts or actual cost incurrence.

        That function is qualitatively different from a traditional interconnection condition. While
the Commission has authority under PURA § 37.0561 to establish standards governing
interconnection, that authority is limited to minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure
costs and maintaining system reliability. 3 A mechanism that collects or retains funds beyond those
impacts implicates ratemaking authority under Chapter 36.

        This concern is further reinforced by the structure of the interconnection process itself.
Interconnection studies are designed to identify system impacts and associated costs, and the
subsequent requirement to execute interconnection agreements and fund CIAC obligations
requires developers to make binding commitments based on those study results. The post-study
CIAC requirement is the point at which development intent is meaningfully tested, because it
requires a binding financial commitment calibrated to actual project costs and informed by
completed study results. Pre-study non-refundability, by contrast, imposes financial exposure
under conditions of uncertainty where withdrawal decisions are driven by study outcomes rather


action is determinative) (citations omitted)).
3
  PURA § 37.0561(b) (“The commission by rule shall establish standards for interconnecting large load customers in
the ERCOT power region in a manner designed to support business development in this state while minimizing the
potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.”).

                                                        3
 than developer conduct.

          Cholla also notes that Commission Staff filed a formal memorandum in related Project No.
59142, recommending that the final rule direct any withheld portion of a financial commitment to
reducing a utility’s annual revenue requirement rather than its rate base. 4 That recommendation
confirms, rather than resolves, the legal concern identified here. The appropriate treatment of
retained funds—whether applied to rate base, annual revenue requirement, or otherwise—is a
discretionary ratemaking determination on which reasonable regulatory judgment can differ. As
such, it is inherently a Chapter 36 issue that must be addressed in a rate proceeding supported by
a full evidentiary record, not predetermined in an interconnection standards rulemaking, regardless
of which specific treatment is selected.

          Accordingly, the relevant inquiry is whether the practical effect of the requirement is
confined to whether it impacts stranded infrastructure risk or system reliability. Because the
proposed framework permits retention and redistribution of funds unrelated to these concerns, it
exceeds that boundary and cannot be sustained solely as an interconnection standard. This
conclusion is reinforced by constitutional considerations.

          In addition, the rule should expressly recognize the statutory limitation reflected in PURA
§ 35.004(c-1), as enacted by Senate Bill (“SB”) 6, which governs the recovery of transmission-
related interconnection costs and applies to interconnection agreements executed on or after the
date SB 6 became effective, which was on June 20, 2025. While § 35.004(c-1) applies directly in
the context of transmission cost recovery, it reflects a broader legislative determination that
interconnection-related financial obligations are to be applied prospectively and in connection with
executed interconnection agreements. Absent explicit clarification, the proposed framework
creates a material risk of retroactive application to projects that executed interconnection
agreements or satisfied interconnection requirements under the prior framework, effectively
subjecting those projects to re-underwriting under a regulatory construct that did not exist at the
time of their development. Such an outcome would undermine regulatory certainty, impair reliance
on existing agreements, and be inconsistent with the Legislature’s express limitation on the
temporal reach of transmission cost recovery obligations.



4
    PUC Proj. No. 59142, Staff Memorandum (Apr. 12, 2026).

                                                       4
         To the extent the proposed rule permits retention of financial security in excess of actual
incurred costs and directs those funds for system-wide benefit, the requirement begins to resemble
a compelled monetary exaction lacking a sufficient nexus to the underlying interconnection
request. The United States Supreme Court has made clear that when the government conditions
regulatory approval on the payment or transfer of property, the condition must bear an “essential
nexus” to a legitimate governmental interest and be “roughly proportional” to the impacts of the
proposed activity. 5 Although these cases arose in the context of individualized permitting decisions
and do not directly address generally applicable regulatory requirements, the underlying nexus and
proportionality principles nonetheless reinforce the requirement that financial obligations imposed
as a condition of interconnection approval bear a demonstrable relationship to the impacts of the
proposed project, including in the context of certain monetary obligations imposed as a condition
of approval. 6

        While the Commission’s objectives—ensuring system reliability and avoiding stranded
infrastructure—are legitimate, the requirements limit the scope of permissible financial obligations
to those reasonably related to the impacts of the specific interconnection request. 7 Where retained
funds exceed actual incurred costs or demonstrable stranded cost exposure, the required payment
is no longer proportional to the burden imposed by the project. Instead, it operates as a transfer of
value for the benefit of the broader system.

        Although the Commission need not resolve constitutional questions in this rulemaking, the
presence of this limitation reinforces the statutory requirement that interconnection-related
financial obligations remain tethered to cost causation under PURA Chapter 36 and § 37.0561,
which require that charges imposed on customers be grounded in the cost of providing service and
the impacts caused by that customer.

        Importantly, the rule already contains a more precise and effective mechanism for testing
development intent. The post-study CIAC requirement is the point at which development intent is

(1994).

may not condition approval of a land-use permit on the applicant’s agreement to fund off-site mitigation without
satisfying nexus and proportionality requirements).
7
  PURA § 35.004(c-1).
7

 meaningfully tested, because it requires a binding financial commitment calibrated to actual
project costs and informed by completed study results. By contrast, pre-study non-refundability
imposes financial exposure under conditions of uncertainty and does not reliably distinguish
speculative behavior from legitimate withdrawal based on study outcomes outside the developer’s
control.

       Therefore, the Commission should revise proposed § 25.194 to provide that financial
security posted at the intermediate agreement stage remains refundable following completion of
the interconnection study, except to the extent necessary to recover actual incurred costs directly
attributable to the interconnection request. Retained amounts should be limited to documented,
non-recoverable costs incurred by the interconnecting utility that cannot be avoided or refunded.

       This refinement also resolves the identified concerns without altering the structure of the
rule. The issue arises from a discrete feature—the treatment of financial security beyond actual
incurred costs—and can be addressed through a single targeted modification. In that form, the rule
preserves financial discipline while ensuring that any retained funds remain tethered to project-
specific costs and within the Commission’s statutory authority.

       This clarification: (i) helps ensure that any funds retained are directly tied to project-
specific costs; (ii) eliminates the retention of excess funds unrelated to the interconnection; and
(iii) removes the need to determine the ratemaking treatment of such funds. At the same time, it
preserves financial discipline, maintains protection against stranded costs, and aligns the rule with
the Commission’s statutory authority while achieving its policy objectives more precisely.

       The overall framework—including the batch study process, financial commitment
structure, milestone requirements, and attestation obligations—is sound and supported. The
concern identified here is narrow, the proposed refinement is straightforward, and the result is a
rule that achieves the Commission’s objectives while remaining firmly within its statutory
authority.

       Cholla submits these comments in a constructive spirit and supports the Commission’s
objectives in this rulemaking. The concerns identified herein are narrow and structural and can be
resolved through a single targeted refinement. Specifically, if intermediate-stage financial security
remains refundable following completion of the interconnection study—except to the extent of
actual incurred costs—then the rule preserves financial discipline, eliminates excess fund

                                                 6
 retention, and operates squarely within the Commission’s statutory authority.

                  III.    STATUTORY FRAMEWORK AND LIMITS ON
                              COMMISSION AUTHORITY

A.     PURA § 37.0561: Scope of Interconnection Standards Authority

       PURA § 37.0561 directs the Commission to establish standards for interconnecting large
load customers in a manner that advances three coequal objectives: supporting business
development, minimizing the risk of stranded infrastructure, and maintaining system reliability.

       The scope of that authority is defined by the statutory focus on “interconnecting” large load
customers. In context, that term refers to the process by which a large load establishes a physical
and operational connection to the transmission system. Although not expressly defined in §
37.0561, its meaning is informed by the statutory objectives themselves, which are tied to system
impacts, infrastructure development, and reliability considerations arising from that connection.
This understanding is reinforced by the ERCOT Planning Guide § 9, which treats interconnection
as a study-driven engineering process involving system impact analysis, identification of required
transmission facilities, and implementation of project-specific upgrades necessary to enable
energization.

       Accordingly, “interconnecting” is most reasonably understood to refer to the physical and
operational integration of a load into the transmission system, rather than to purely financial or
administrative constructs. Financial requirements adopted pursuant to § 37.0561 must therefore
remain reasonably related to that process, including the costs, risks, and system impacts directly
attributable to the interconnection request. This includes requirements that demonstrate project
viability, ensure that developers are financially capable of proceeding, and protect utilities from
unrecovered interconnection-related costs. It does not include authority to determine how funds
are applied to system-wide cost recovery after the interconnection process has concluded or been
abandoned.

       This limitation applies with particular force at the intermediate agreement stage, where
system impacts, required facilities, and associated costs have not yet been determined. At that
stage, financial requirements may serve as a demonstration of project viability, but must remain
provisional in nature and may not function as mechanisms for cost recovery, value transfer, or


                                                 7
 retention of funds beyond those necessary to recover actual costs incurred, independent of
identified system impacts or study results.

        Under Texas law, statutory authority is defined by the plain meaning of the text. 8 The plain
meaning of § 37.0561 does not extend to ratemaking determinations. Thus, the scope of the
Commission’s authority under PURA § 37.0561 must be defined by the ordinary meaning of the
statutory terms used by the Legislature.

B.      PURA § 35.004: Cost Causation as a Limiting Principle

        Although PURA § 35.004 governs wholesale transmission service, it reflects a broader and
well-established cost-causation principle—that costs incurred to serve a specific customer request
should be recovered from that customer and not shifted to others. 9 This principle is foundational
to Texas utility regulation and is likewise embedded in PURA Chapter 36, which requires that rates
and charges be just and reasonable and grounded in the cost of providing service. 10 Moreover,
Texas courts have consistently recognized that cost allocation must bear a reasonable relationship
to the service provided or the burden imposed. 11

        Consistent with PURA § 37.0561, interconnection-related financial obligations must
therefore be tied to the actual system impacts and costs attributable to the large load customer’s
request. This principle provides the only administrable limiting standard for financial obligations
imposed under the rule. Under the proposed rule, however, financial security may be retained even
where no interconnection facilities are constructed and no stranded costs are incurred. In such
circumstances, the retained funds do not correspond to any cost caused by the developer, but
instead are applied to reduce system-wide transmission costs. That result is not a function of
interconnection cost recovery, but of cost allocation, and therefore falls within the domain
governed by Chapter 36. That outcome departs from cost-causation principles and is more
appropriately characterized as a system-wide cost allocation determination governed by Chapter
36.

432, 439 (Tex. 2011) (holding that unambiguous statutory language must be interpreted according to its plain
meaning); Entergy Gulf States, Inc. v. Summers, 282 S.W.3d 433, 437 (Tex. 2009).
9
  See PURA § 35.004(c).
10
   See PURA §§ 36.003, 36.004.
11
   See City of Corpus Christi v. Pub. Util. Comm'n of Tex., 51 S.W.3d 231 (Tex. 2001) (per curiam); see also Public
Utility Commission v. Gulf States Utilities Co., 809 S.W.2d 201, 207–08 (Tex. 1991).

                                                        8
 This conclusion is further reinforced by the prospective framework reflected in PURA § 35.004(c-
1), governing transmission-related interconnection cost recovery and applicable interconnection
agreements executed on or after June 20, 2025. While that provision applies directly in the
transmission cost recovery context, it reflects a legislative determination that interconnection-
related financial obligations should be tied to specific agreements and applied prospectively, rather
than imposed retroactively or independent of identified costs..

C.       PURA Chapter 36: Ratemaking Authority and Process

         PURA Chapter 36 governs how utilities recover costs from ratepayers. It requires the
Commission to establish rates based on a cost-of-service framework that includes:

         1. Determination of invested capital;
         2. Evaluation of prudence and necessity of costs;
         3. Allocation of costs among customer classes; and
         4. Findings that resulting rates are just and reasonable. 12

         As proposed, proposed § 25.194 bypasses this framework by mandating how retained funds
must be applied in future rate proceedings. Whether those funds reduce rate base or annual revenue
requirement, the rule predetermines a ratemaking outcome without the evidentiary process
required by Chapter 36 and without the record necessary to evaluate cost responsibility, allocation,
or prudence.

Because the rule permits retention of funds beyond those tied to actual interconnection costs, it
necessarily requires a determination as to how those excess funds are treated for ratemaking
purposes. That determination is inherently a Chapter 36 function and cannot be predetermined in
an interconnection standards rulemaking. This is not a procedural issue; it is a substantive
limitation on Commission authority.

D.       Harmonization of Statutory Provisions

         Texas courts require that statutes be read harmoniously so as to give effect to each provision
where possible. 13 When read together, PURA § 37.0561 governs the standards applicable to large


12
  See PURA §§ 36.003, 36.051, 36.053.
13
  See e.g., Fort Worth Transp. Auth. v. Rodriguez, 830, 850 (Tex. 2018) (stating that courts strive to give the statutory
provision a meaning that is in harmony with other related statutes); see also Helena Chem. Co. v. Wilkins, 47 S.W.3d
486, 493 (Tex. 2001) (stating that courts must always consider the statute as a whole rather than its isolated provisions).

                                                            9
 load interconnection, while Chapter 36 governs the recovery and allocation of system-wide
transmission costs through the Commission’s ratemaking process, including the determination of
revenue requirement and cost allocation among customer classes.

           As proposed, the rule disrupts this statutory structure by using interconnection standards to
predetermine the allocation of costs at a system-wide level. A mechanism that permits retention of
funds beyond those tied to the interconnection request and directs their application to reduce
overall transmission cost recovery operates within the domain of Chapter 36 ratemaking. Nothing
in § 37.0561 authorizes the Commission to make such determinations through an interconnection
standards rulemaking.

                     IV.      STRUCTURAL DEFICIENCY IN THE PROPOSED
                                   FINANCIAL FRAMEWORK

           The legal defect is that the proposed financial security framework effects a system-wide
cost allocation and predetermines the treatment of utility revenues outside a Chapter 36 ratemaking
proceeding, thereby exceeding the Commission’s authority under PURA § 37.0561 and departing
from cost-based ratemaking requirements.

           This defect does not arise from any single provision, but from the interaction of two
elements: (i) pre-study non-refundable financial security; and (ii) the mandatory application of
retained funds to reduce transmission cost recovery. When combined, these features produce a
mechanism in which:

               1. Funds are collected before interconnection costs are known or incurred;
               2. Funds may be retained irrespective of whether such costs are ever incurred; and
               3. Retained funds are applied to reduce system-wide transmission costs.

It is this interaction—not any single element—that produces the legal defect.

           Under established administrative law principles, agency action must be evaluated based on
the rationale and legal authority supporting it, and may not be sustained on grounds that extend
beyond the scope of that authority.14 Consistent with this principle, Texas courts require that
agency action be supported by statutory authority and a rational basis and may not result in



14
     See SEC v. Chenery Corp., 332 U.S. 194, 196 (1947).

                                                           10
 arbitrary or unsupported cost allocation. 15

        Here, regardless of how the requirement is characterized, the practical effect of the
proposed mechanism is to collect and redistribute funds in a manner that implicates system-wide
cost allocation. That effect must fall within the Commission’s statutory authority under PURA §
37.0561 and Chapter 36; it cannot be justified solely by labeling the requirement as an
interconnection condition. Where the rule operates to retain and reallocate funds beyond those tied
to the costs or impacts of a specific interconnection request, it departs from cost-based ratemaking
principles and exceeds the bounds of permissible regulatory action.

        This structure is fundamentally different from traditional interconnection cost recovery
mechanisms, such as contribution in aid of construction (“CIAC”), which are directly tied to
facilities constructed for, and costs caused by, a specific customer. CIAC obligations arise only
after study completion, are calibrated to identified facilities and costs, and require payment based
on actual system impacts. They therefore function as a precise cost-causation mechanism and do
not produce excess funds available for redistribution or application to broader system costs. By
contrast, the proposed financial security framework imposes and permits retention of funds prior
to that determination and without ensuring a corresponding relationship to incurred costs, thereby
departing from the cost-causation principle that governs interconnection cost recovery.

        The defect is therefore structural: the rule transforms a project-specific interconnection
requirement into a system-wide cost allocation mechanism untethered from actual costs incurred
or impacts caused. This conclusion does not depend on the Commission’s policy objectives or on
the broader structure of the rule, both of which are supported. Rather, it arises from the treatment
of financial security in excess of actual incurred costs. Importantly, this defect is not dependent on
the magnitude of the financial security requirement or the percentage subject to forfeiture; it arises
from the absence of a limiting principle tying retained funds to actual incurred costs.

        This issue is resolved if financial security is refundable except to the extent of actual
incurred costs. Under such a structure:

             1. Funds correspond directly to identifiable costs;
             2. No excess funds are retained or redistributed; and

15
  See Public Utility Commission v. Gulf States Utilities Co., 809 S.W.2d 201, 207–08 (Tex. 1991); Texas Industrial
Energy Consumers v. CenterPoint Energy Houston Electric, LLC, 324 S.W.3d 95, 105–06 (Tex. 2010).

                                                       11
              3. No ratemaking determination is required outside a Chapter 36 proceeding.

In that form, the requirement operates as a permissible interconnection standard consistent with
PURA § 37.0561, rather than as an unauthorized ratemaking mechanism.

                     V.       EVIDENTIARY AND POLICY DEFICIENCIES

        The PFP does not identify an evidentiary basis demonstrating that the required financial
security amounts bear a reasonable relationship to actual interconnection costs or to any
quantifiable measure of system risk. The record does not include a cost study, empirical analysis,
historical interconnection data, or other quantitative support for the $50,000 per MW requirement
or for the proportion of funds subject to forfeiture. Nor does it explain how those amounts
correspond to expected study costs, facility costs, or stranded infrastructure exposure associated
with large load interconnection.

        This omission is material. Under Texas law, agency rules must be grounded in statutory
authority and supported by a rational basis reflected in the record. 16 In the ratemaking context,
courts likewise require that cost allocations bear a reasonable relationship to the costs incurred and
the service provided. 17 Although the instant rule is framed as an interconnection standard under
PURA § 37.0561, it imposes financial obligations on customers; as such, those obligations must
still be supported by a rational, cost-based justification consistent with Chapter 36 principles.

        The absence of such support indicates that the proposed financial security requirement is
not calibrated to recover interconnection-related costs or to reflect measurable system risk. Instead,
the requirement operates as a fixed, ex ante financial obligation untethered from the costs or
impacts of any specific project. This disconnect reinforces the structural concern identified above:
the mechanism is not functioning as a cost recovery tool, but instead operates as a generalized
financial screen that may generate retained funds unrelated to actual interconnection costs.

        The policy justification offered for this structure—deterring speculative interconnection
requests—is legitimate. However, the effectiveness of that mechanism must be evaluated in light
of the existing interconnection framework. The proposed rule relies on pre-study non-refundability



16
   See Public Utility Commission v. Gulf States Utilities Co., 809 S.W.2d 201, 207–08 (Tex. 1991) (requiring that
Commission action be supported by substantial evidence and not be arbitrary or capricious).
17
   See City of Corpus Christi v. Pub. Util. Comm'n of Tex., 51 S.W.3d 231 (Tex. 2001) (per curiam).

                                                       12
 imposed at a stage when neither the developer nor the utility has sufficient information to evaluate
project feasibility or system impacts. At that stage, withdrawal decisions are driven primarily by
study outcomes, which are outside the developer’s control. As a result, the forfeiture mechanism
does not reliably distinguish between speculative projects and projects that are withdrawn based
on newly identified system constraints or costs, and therefore provides limited incremental
screening value.

       In addition, the intermediate agreement framework should not be interpreted or applied as
a discretionary gating mechanism that delays access to interconnection studies pending satisfaction
of commercial or financial conditions beyond those necessary to demonstrate project viability.
Planning Guide § 9 establishes a sequencing framework in which interconnection studies inform
system planning. The introduction of intermediate agreement requirements should not disrupt that
structure by conditioning study initiation on requirements that are not directly tied to study
readiness. Financial security at this stage should function as evidence of project credibility and
commitment, not as a prerequisite that delays or restricts timely study progression.

       By contrast, the framework already incorporates more precise and effective mechanisms
for screening speculative projects. The batch study process under development is designed to
produce system impact results, and the subsequent requirement to execute interconnection
agreements and fund CIAC obligations requires developers to make binding commitments based
on complete and project-specific information. The post-study CIAC requirement is the point at
which development intent is meaningfully tested, because it requires a binding financial
commitment calibrated to actual project costs and informed by completed study results. Those
post-study commitments directly reflect the costs and risks associated with the project and
therefore provide a more accurate indicator of development intent. Projects that cannot support
those commitments will not proceed, thereby achieving the Commission’s objective without
imposing pre-study financial penalties untethered from cost causation.

       Pre-study non-refundability, by comparison, introduces significant financial exposure
under conditions of uncertainty. It does not calibrate the level of risk to the magnitude of system
impact, or account for differences among projects. As a result, it may deter legitimate
development—particularly      capital-intensive    or   infrastructure-dependent   projects—while
providing limited additional screening value beyond that already achieved through the study and


                                                  13
 CIAC processes.

           In sum, the PFP does not demonstrate that the proposed financial security requirement is
supported by a sufficient evidentiary basis or that it is reasonably tailored to achieve its stated
policy objective. A structure that limits financial exposure to actual incurred costs and relies on
post-study commitments to demonstrate project viability would better align with both statutory
requirements and sound regulatory policy.

                  VI.      FAILURE OF ALTERNATIVE LEGAL JUSTIFICATIONS

           The structural concerns identified in these comments are not resolved by recasting the
proposed financial mechanism under alternative legal theories. Regardless of how it is
characterized, none of the proffered justifications supports the combined operation of (i) non-
refundable financial security at the pre-study stage, and (ii) the mandatory application of retained
funds to transmission cost recovery. Critically, none of these theories supplies a principled limiting
standard grounded in the statutory text, nor do they reconcile the mechanism with the cost-based
ratemaking requirements of PURA Chapter 36 or the Commission’s authority under PURA §
37.0561.

           First, the characterization of the forfeiture mechanism as a regulatory penalty is not
supported under PURA. Regulatory penalties must be tied to violations of statutory or regulatory
obligations and must be imposed pursuant to express authority, such as PURA § 15.023.
Withdrawal of an interconnection request is not a violation; it is an expressly contemplated and
procedurally accommodated outcome within the rule itself. Imposing substantial financial
forfeiture in the absence of any violation transforms the mechanism into a penalty without statutory
authorization. Moreover, any penalty must be reasonably related to the conduct or harm it is
intended to address and supported by a rational basis in the record; otherwise, it risks being
arbitrary or beyond the Commission’s statutory authority. 18 Here, the rule imposes identical
forfeiture consequences regardless of whether a developer acted in bad faith or withdrew due to
adverse study results outside its control. That lack of proportionality further undermines any
penalty-based justification.

           Second, the “filed rate” doctrine affords presumptive validity to rates and charges


18
     See Gulf States Utilities, 809 S.W.2d at 207–08.

                                                        14
 established by a regulator acting within the scope of its statutory authority and prohibits collateral
challenges to those approved rates; it reflects the principle that rates must be set through the
regulator’s prescribed ratemaking process and applied uniformly to similarly situated customers.
The doctrine does not create or expand that authority, nor does it permit an agency to impose
charges outside the statutory framework that governs ratemaking. Accordingly, the doctrine does
not apply where the agency lacks the power to impose the charge in the first instance. 19 Consistent
with Texas law, agency action must be grounded in statutory authority and supported by a rational
basis; charges imposed outside that authority are not insulated by deference doctrines. 20

        Next, reliance on the filed rate doctrine does not resolve the underlying concern. The
doctrine affords presumptive validity to rates and charges established within the scope of an
agency’s statutory authority; it does not validate actions that exceed that authority. 21 The issue
presented here is precisely a question of statutory authority—whether the Commission may require
retention of funds beyond actual interconnection costs and direct their application to system-wide
cost recovery through this rulemaking. The filed rate doctrine presupposes, rather than establishes,
that such authority exists.

        Third, the Commission’s general market design authority under PURA § 39.151 does not
extend to the mechanism at issue. Section 39.151 governs the operation and design of the
wholesale market and the functions of ERCOT; it does not authorize the imposition of financial

A.     PURA § 37.0561: Scope of Interconnection Standards Authority

       PURA § 37.0561 directs the Commission to establish standards for interconnecting large
load customers in a manner that advances three coequal obj ectives: supporting business
development, minimizing the risk of stranded infrastructure, and maintaining system reliability.

       The scope ofthat authority is defined by the statutory focus on "interconnecting" large load
customers. In context, that term refers to the process by which a large load establishes a physical
and operational connection to the transmission system. Although not expressly defined in §
37.0561, its meaning is informed by the statutory objectives themselves, which are tied to system
impacts, infrastructure development, and reliability considerations arising from that connection.
This understanding is reinforced by the ERCOT Planning Guide § 9, which treats interconnection
as a study-driven engineering process involving system impact analysis, identification of required
transmission facilities, and implementation of project-specific upgrades necessary to enable
energization.

       Accordingly, "interconnecting" is most reasonably understood to refer to the physical and
operational integration of a load into the transmission system, rather than to purely financial or
administrative constructs. Financial requirements adopted pursuant to § 37.0561 must therefore
remain reasonably related to that process, including the costs, risks, and system impacts directly
attributable to the interconnection request. This includes requirements that demonstrate proj ect
viability, ensure that developers are financially capable of proceeding, and protect utilities from
unrecovered interconnection-related costs. It does not include authority to determine how funds
are applied to system-wide cost recovery after the interconnection process has concluded or been
abandoned.
       This limitation applies with particular force at the intermediate agreement stage, where
system impacts, required facilities, and associated costs have not yet been determined. At that
stage, financial requirements may serve as a demonstration of proj ect viability, but must remain
provisional in nature and may not function as mechanisms for cost recovery, value transfer, or


                                                1
 retention of funds beyond those necessary to recover actual costs incurred, independent of
identified system impacts or study results.

         Under Texas law, statutory authority is defined by the plain meaning of the text. 8 The plain
meaning of § 37.0561 does not extend to ratemaking determinations. Thus, the scope of the
Commission's authority under PURA § 37.0561 must be defined by the ordinary meaning of the
statutory terms used by the Legislature.

B.       PURA § 35.004: Cost Causation as a Limiting Principle

         Although PURA § 35.004 governs wholesale transmission service, it reflects a broader and
well-established cost-causation principle-that costs incurred to serve a specific customer request
should be recovered from that customer and not shifted to others.' This principle is foundational
to Texas utility regulation and is likewise embedded in PURA Chapter 36, which requires that rates

                           VII.      CONSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS

         The proposed forfeiture mechanism also raises a serious constitutional concern under the
regulatory takings framework. While the Commission is not required at this stage to resolve
constitutional questions definitively, the presence of a substantial constitutional issue is
independently relevant under established principles of statutory construction.

A.       Penn Central

         Under a pivotal U. S. Supreme Court Case-Penn Central Transportation Co. v. Cio' of
New York-regulatory action may constitute a taking where it imposes a significant economic
burden, interferes with reasonable investment-backed expectations, and involves a transfer a
government action of a character not sufficiently tied to the public interest. 24 The proposed rule
presents each of these elements. The economic impact is substantial. Developers may be required
to forfeit tens of millions of dollars in circumstances where no interconnection facilities are
constructed and no corresponding costs are incurred. This is not a fee for service or a recovery of
costs; it is a compelled transfer of capital.

B.       Unconstitutional Conditions Doctrine

         These concerns are reinforced by the unconstitutional conditions doctrine, under which
monetary obligations imposed as a condition of regulatory approval must bear an "essential nexus"




24 Penn Central Transportation Co . v. City of New York 438 U
                                                            - . S. 104 ( 1978 ).

                                                           17
 and "rough proportionality" to the impacts of the regulated activity. 25 To the extent financial
security is retained in excess of actual incurred costs, the retained amount is not proportionate to
any identifiable impact of the interconnection request, but instead operates as a transfer of value
for broader system benefit. Texas courts recognize analogous limitations under the Texas
Constitution's takings clause. 26

C.        Constitutional Avoidance Canon

          Under the constitutional avoidance canon, where a statute is susceptible to more than one
reasonable interpretation, courts adopt the interpretation that avoids serious constitutional
concerns.27 That principle applies here. PURA § 37.0561 can be construed either to permit
retention of funds beyond actual costs or to limit financial obligations to cost-based recovery. The
latter construction avoids the constitutional concern entirely.

D.        Reasonable Investment-Backed Expectations

          The rule also interferes with reasonable investment-backed expectations. Developers
entering the interconnection process have a reasonable expectation, grounded in longstanding cost
causation principles and in the rule's own withdrawal provisions, that financial security will be
used to recover actual costs incurred in connection with their request. The imposition of forfeiture
based on study outcomes-rather than developer conduct-disrupts that expectation. Many
developers seeking interconnection of Large Loads have already received financing and have
expended funds in reliance on the cost-causation principle being honored.

          A structure in which financial security is refundable except for actual incurred costs does
not raise the same constitutional issue, because retained funds correspond directly to identifiable
costs incurred in connection with the interconnection request. The constitutional concern arises
only where funds are retained without such a nexus.
